title: Mechanistic Interpretability for Steering Vision-Language-Action Models
venue: CoRL 2025 (9th Conference on Robot Learning, Seoul)
action_head: discrete action tokens (OpenVLA bins and pi0-FAST FAST tokens; the steered 'pi0' is pi0-FAST, not the flow-matching pi0)
methods: FFN value-vector projection onto token vocabulary (Geva et al. 2022)
manual and kNN clustering of value vectors by top-token semantics
activation steering by overwriting FFN neuron activations with a fixed scalar
two-proportion z-test on top tokens before/after fine-tuning
question: Do VLAs keep semantically interpretable FFN neurons after action training, and can upweighting concept-aligned neurons (fast/slow, up/low/high) steer robot motion at inference time without fine-tuning?
key_findings: Using the Geva et al. criterion (>=4 of top-30 tokens share a pattern, 10 random value vectors per layer), pi0 and its base PaliGemma show interpretable and semantic value vectors at similar rates; the paper claims fewer than 25% of FFN neurons are rewired for action prediction (Fig. 2a).
Action tokens appear among the top-100 tokens of value vectors in every layer of OpenVLA and pi0, most at the final layer; authors read this as no hard 'task then control' transition (Fig. 2b).

Fine-tuning pi0-FAST on DROID mainly changes action tokens in value vectors (more uneven distribution); the top-200 DROID instruction tokens appear 1.2x more often after fine-tuning (mean z = 1.0) (Fig. 3, App. B.2).

OpenVLA on LIBERO-Long: 'fast' clusters produce larger end-effector displacement than 'slow' clusters by 27.73% on average, max 148.54%; all 10 matched comparisons p < 0.001 (paired t-test), Cohen's d from -0.091 to 1.419 (sweep: cluster sizes 10/20, coefficients 2-20, 10 tasks x 10 rollouts).
Depth: 'up' clusters injected in all layers give mean Y displacement 0.098, late layers 0.086, early layers 0.007; late vs full d = -0.062 (negligible).

Real UR5 with pi0-FAST: 'low' and 'slow' interventions produce the lowest / slowest motion, but 'high' and 'fast' look like the no-intervention baseline; random-vector steering differs little from no intervention; prompt prefixes ('low ...', 'slow safe ...') have a weaker effect than steering (Fig. 7, box plots over 10 rollouts).

evidence.setting: both (simulation with OpenVLA; real UR5 with pi0-FAST)
benchmarks: two custom UR5 pick-and-place tasks (Low/High Transport, 75 demos; Slow/Fast Transport, 120 demos)
evidence.scale: Sim: 10 tasks x 10 rollouts per configuration, deterministic seeding. Real: 10 rollouts per steering variant and baseline. Interpretability statistics on 10 randomly sampled value vectors per layer.
evidence.statistics: partial: paired t-tests and Cohen's d in simulation; real-robot results are box plots only, no tests; no CIs
evidence.baselines: no intervention, prompt modification with concept words, random six-vector upweighting (real robot only); slow vs fast clusters compared against each other in sim

causal_validation: Yes, by steering: overwriting the activations of concept-aligned FFN neurons changes end-effector displacement (sim) and max height / speed (real). There is a random-neuron control only on the real robot. No ablation of the clusters and no test that steering preserves task success.
closed_loop: Partly. LIBERO steering and the real Low/High task are closed-loop rollouts. The real Slow/Fast result is NOT closed-loop: all variants are computed in parallel but only the un-steered baseline action is executed, so speed is measured on predicted actions along the baseline trajectory.
limitations_stated: Clusters are built from token similarity, not behavior, and can conflate distinct behaviors (e.g. 'slow and careful' vs 'slow and stuck').
Meaning of value vectors drifts across models, tasks and time; an 'up' vector may act differently elsewhere.
Only pick-and-place with one arm; mobile, bimanual and unstructured settings not tested.
critique: The abstract says 'pi0', but all steering is on discrete-token models (OpenVLA, pi0-FAST); nothing here shows that FFN-neuron steering works on a flow-matching action expert, where the VLM's FFN outputs never pass through a vocabulary head.
Task success under steering is never reported, so we cannot tell whether faster/higher motion comes with broken task execution.
Only one direction of each pair works on the real robot (low and slow, not high and fast); with 10 rollouts and no tests this is a weak, asymmetric effect.

Sim results compare fast vs slow clusters with each other, not with a random-neuron or no-intervention baseline, so 'semantic' specificity is not isolated in simulation; 'all significant' with d as low as -0.091 suggests very large paired samples or a sign inconsistency.
The '<25% of neurons rewired' and 'largely semantic' claims rest on 10 hand-labelled vectors per layer, a small and subjective sample.
The Slow/Fast open-loop measurement means the real-robot speed claim does not show the behavior a steered robot would actually produce.
code: not released (only the openpi codebase is linked)
one_line: Projecting VLA FFN neurons onto the vocabulary finds concept neurons like 'slow' and 'low', and upweighting them shifts OpenVLA motion in LIBERO and pi0-FAST motion on a UR5, though only some directions work and task success is not reported.
